610.title: Cast your care (1 Peter 5:7)
610.hook: casting all your care upon him, for he hath care of you
610.howItsDone: Catholics bring their worries to God in personal prayer, in intentions offered at Mass and in devotions of trust in Divine Providence; the tradition calls the habit of entrusting everything to God abandonment to providence.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a royal priesthood: every baptized person, offering the day itself to God. Your line was a royal priesthood.

On the road into Jerusalem, a few days before he dies, Jesus needs something to ride. The disciples bring a young colt, and Luke says they throw their cloaks onto it and set Jesus on top. Throw. Not fold, not drape. They toss their coats on the animal's back, the way you'd sling a bag onto a bed after a long day. Peter uses the same Greek verb near the end of his first letter, and he isn't talking about coats.
screen: `CLOAKS THROWN ON A COLT.` → `THE SAME GREEK VERB.` → `PETER USES IT AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse in the Douay-Rheims: "Casting all your care upon him, for he hath care of you." Casting: throwing it on, the way the disciples threw their cloaks onto the colt. Not a polite handing over, but a toss, the move of someone who's been carrying something too long. And it's all your care, not just the small worries you'd be willing to share. Notice the word care appears twice, and in Greek it's two different words. The first is merimna: anxiety, worry that won't sit still. Jesus uses the same family of words in the Sermon on the Mount, when he tells his followers not to be anxious about tomorrow. The second is softer: it matters to him. Literally, you are a concern to him. So the sentence runs: throw your anxiety on him, because you matter to him. The reason isn't that worry is foolish. The reason is that someone cares. Peter didn't invent this. He's echoing the psalms, which the Douay-Rheims renders: "Cast thy care upon the Lord, and he shall sustain thee." And look at the verse just before: be humbled under the mighty hand of God. In Peter's order, casting your care is a kind of humility: admitting you can't carry everything alone, and letting someone else take the weight. Catholic spiritual writers have a name for the habit: abandonment to God's providence.

611.title: The roaring lion (1 Peter 5:8–9)
611.hook: be sober and watch: read every Tuesday at night prayer
611.tomorrow: a thousand years as a day
611.howItsDone: In the Liturgy of the Hours, Night Prayer (Compline) begins with an examination of conscience and, on Tuesdays, has 1 Peter 5:8–9 as its short reading; priests, religious and some lay Catholics pray it before sleep.

segments.voice: Yesterday, merimna: worry thrown on God like a cloak onto a colt. Your line was he hath care of you.

It's late on a Tuesday. In a monastery chapel, a convent, a hospital break room, a bedroom with a phone propped on the pillow, people are praying the last prayer of the Church's day, called Compline, or Night Prayer. The lights are low. The psalm is done. And the short reading for Tuesday night is two verses from the end of First Peter. In the older form of the prayer, those same verses opened Compline every night, right before the lights go out.
screen: `LATE ON A TUESDAY.` → `NIGHT PRAYER: COMPLINE.` → `TWO VERSES BEFORE LIGHTS OUT.`

segments.voice: Here they are in the Douay-Rheims: "Be sober and watch: because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, goeth about seeking whom he may devour." Two commands first. Be sober: the Greek means clear-headed, not drunk, not foggy. And watch: stay awake, keep alert. That second word has a history for Peter. On the night before Jesus died, in the garden of Gethsemane, Jesus asked Peter to watch with him for one hour. Peter fell asleep, more than once. Now the same man, years later, tells the whole Church: stay awake. Then the picture: a lion, prowling, roaring, looking for someone to swallow. A prowler in the dark is a night fear, which is one reason the verse sits well at bedtime. The Church teaches that the devil is real, a fallen creature, but a creature: not God's equal, with limits on what he can do. So Peter doesn't say run, or panic. He says, "Whom resist ye, strong in faith." Stand your ground. And he adds something easy to miss: your brothers and sisters all over the world are going through the same sufferings. In the picture, the lion looks for the one who's alone. The answer is a clear head, open eyes, and a whole flock. Night Prayer is shaped for this. It begins with a short look back over the day, and it ends by entrusting the night to God.

segments.voice: Sit up a little, as if keeping watch, and walk back through today, slowly, from now to this morning: where you were clear-headed, where you drifted, scrolled or snapped. Don't judge it, just see it, the way a watchman sees the walls, and notice one moment you'd like to handle differently tomorrow. If you pray, hand the night to God, or pray a line from Compline if you know one; if not, close the day with your eyes open to it.
Compline, the Church's last prayer of the day. Where First Peter's warning about the roaring lion is read, right before the lights go out. Today's word.
Your line: be sober, watch. Clear-headed, awake, and never the one left alone. Good night.

612.title: A thousand years as a day (2 Peter 3:8–9)
612.hook: God is patient, not willing that any should perish
612.howItsDone: Catholics profess at every Mass that Christ will come again in glory, and Advent each year is a season of joyful waiting; the Church reads God's patience as time given for conversion.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Compline: be sober, watch, and resist the roaring lion, strong in faith. Your line was be sober, watch.

In October you push tulip bulbs into cold dirt, cover them, and walk away. Then nothing. All winter the bed looks exactly like a patch of mud. A neighbor walking by would swear nothing is happening there. Underneath, roots are going down in the dark, on a schedule no one can hurry. By the time the second letter of Peter was written, Christians had been waiting a long time for Christ to come back in glory. The first generation was dying. And people were starting to look at the patch of mud and laugh.
screen: `BULBS IN COLD DIRT.` → `ALL WINTER, NOTHING TO SEE.` → `PEOPLE START TO LAUGH.`

segments.voice: Peter quotes the mockers almost word for word. Where is this promised coming? Ever since our fathers fell asleep, everything goes on just as it always has. It's a reasonable complaint, and the letter takes it seriously, in two parts. First, time. In the Douay-Rheims: "one day with the Lord is as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day." Peter is borrowing from Psalm eighty-nine, ninety in most modern Bibles, which says a thousand years in God's sight are like yesterday, gone. God doesn't stand inside the clock the way people do. What feels like forever from the mud is a single day from above. Second, and this is the heart of it, the delay has a reason, and the reason is mercy. The Lord isn't slow about his promise, Peter says, as some think. He is being patient with you, "not willing that any should perish, but that all should return to penance." Return to penance is the Douay-Rheims way of saying turn around, change your heart. The Greek word for patient here is makrothymei, literally long-tempered. Everyone knows short-tempered: the flash, the snap. God, in this verse, is the opposite. His fuse is a thousand years long. So the waiting isn't absence. It's room: room for one more person to turn around, and maybe that person is the one doing the laughing. The Church still lives inside this waiting, and every Mass looks forward to his coming. But Peter's letter turns the question around: the delay may be the kindest thing that's happening.

If you pray, ask for some of God's long temper; if not, just let the timeline grow longer.

613.title: What we have handled (1 John 1:1–4)
613.hook: the word of life that we have seen and touched
613.howItsDone: Catholic sacraments are celebrated with things that can be seen and touched, water, oil, bread, wine and the laying on of hands, and Catholics may keep a rosary, cross or medal close as a physical reminder of their faith.

segments.voice: Yesterday, makrothymei: a God with a very long fuse. Your line was he is patient.

You can read everything about the ocean, tides, salt, the color of deep water, and watch it in videos for hours. Then one day you stand at the edge and a cold wave runs over your feet, and the water teaches what the books couldn't. Hearing about it, seeing it, touching it: three different kinds of knowing. The first letter of John doesn't open with a greeting or a name. It opens with a witness, an old man, as tradition pictures him, saying: I'm not passing on a rumor. I was there. I touched him.
screen: `READING ABOUT THE OCEAN.` → `A COLD WAVE OVER YOUR FEET.` → `I WAS THERE. I TOUCHED HIM.`

segments.voice: Listen to the sentence move, in the Douay-Rheims: "That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we have looked upon, and our hands have handled, of the word of life." It starts at the very start of everything, from the beginning, an echo of the opening of John's Gospel. Then it comes closer, step by step. Heard: across a room. Seen: now he's in view. Looked upon: a long, steady gaze. And handled: hands on. The Word that was with God from the beginning is something a fisherman could put his hand on. Why insist? Some scholars think the letter was answering people who said Jesus only seemed to have a body, that God would never really take on flesh, get tired, bleed. John won't have it. Later in the letter he says that every spirit which confesses Jesus Christ come in the flesh is of God. The Greek word for handled is the same one the risen Jesus uses in Luke's Gospel, when the frightened disciples think he's a spirit: handle, and see. And notice why John writes: so that you may have fellowship with us, and our fellowship is with the Father and with his Son. The Greek is koinonia, which comes into Catholic language as communion. And so that our joy may be full. For Catholics this touchable faith runs through the sacraments: water on a forehead, oil on hands, bread placed on a tongue or in a palm. God, in this tradition, keeps coming close enough to touch.

Let it stand for a faith that says God came close enough to touch. If you pray, hold it as a prayer without words; if not, stay with the plain fact of touch and notice what your hands know.

614.title: If we confess (1 John 1:8–9)
614.hook: if we say we have no sin we deceive ourselves
614.howItsDone: Catholics confess their sins together in the penitential act near the start of Mass, and individually in the sacrament of Penance, where a person names their sins to a priest and receives absolution; the Church asks Catholics to confess serious sins at least once a year.

segments.voice: Yesterday, koinonia: the word of life, heard, seen and handled. Your line was seen and touched.

A map app can get you almost anywhere, on one condition: it has to know where you actually are. If the little blue dot thinks you're downtown when you're stuck on a country road, every direction it gives you will be wrong too, no matter how confident the voice sounds. It can't route you home from a place you're pretending to be. A few lines into his first letter, John says something very like this about the soul. And he says it to believers, not to strangers.
screen: `THE BLUE DOT HAS TO BE RIGHT.` → `NO ROUTE FROM A PRETEND PLACE.` → `JOHN SAYS IT TO BELIEVERS.`

segments.voice: The Douay-Rheims: "If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us." Notice the we. John doesn't point at outsiders; he includes himself, the one who touched the word of life. The danger isn't sin so much as pretending, putting the blue dot somewhere it isn't. Then the turn: "If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just, to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all iniquity." The Greek word for confess is homologeo, and some readers hear two pieces in it, same and say: to confess is to say the same thing, to agree with God about what actually happened. Not to grovel, not to perform, just to stop arguing with the truth. Then John picks two surprising words for God. Faithful, because God promised to forgive and keeps his promises. And just. You might expect justice to stand in the way of forgiveness. John puts it on forgiveness's side. A few verses later he explains: we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ, who is the atonement for our sins. Catholics hear this passage in several places. Near the start of Mass, in what's called the penitential act, the people confess together that they have sinned, before they hear the word. And in the sacrament of Penance, a person names their sins to a priest and hears the words of absolution. The Catechism quotes these very verses when it says that to receive God's mercy, we have to admit our faults. Mercy can't reach a place you insist you aren't standing.

615.title: In deed and in truth (1 John 3:18)
615.hook: let us not love in word, but in deed
615.howItsDone: Catholics practice love in deed through the corporal works of mercy, such as feeding the hungry, sheltering the homeless and visiting the sick and imprisoned, often through parishes, Catholic charities and groups like the Society of Saint Vincent de Paul.

segments.voice: Yesterday, homologeo: saying the same thing as the truth, and a God faithful to forgive. Your line was he is faithful to forgive.

At their wedding, she said beautiful things. Decades later, nobody remembers the vows word for word. What the grandchildren remember is that every winter morning, before she left for work, he went out in the cold, scraped the ice off her windshield and started the car so it would be warm. He was not a man of speeches. He rarely said I love you out loud. He scraped that windshield every icy morning, for decades. John, in his first letter, has been talking about love. And then he says the thing that windshield was saying.
screen: `BEAUTIFUL VOWS, LONG FORGOTTEN.` → `EVERY ICY MORNING, A WINDSHIELD.` → `JOHN SAYS THE SAME THING.`

segments.voice: First John sets it up with Christ himself. We know what love is, he says, because Jesus laid down his life for us, and so we ought to lay down our lives for each other. That's the high bar. Then he brings it straight down to the kitchen table. The Douay-Rheims: "He that hath the substance of this world, and shall see his brother in need, and shall shut up his bowels from him: how doth the charity of God abide in him?" Bowels sounds strange now, but the Greek word, splanchna, means your insides, your gut, the place Greek speakers located compassion. In plain English: shut his heart. You see someone in need, you feel that tug in your gut, and you close the door on it. John asks how God's love could possibly be living there. Then the line: "My little children, let us not love in word, nor in tongue, but in deed, and in truth." Two pairs. Not word and tongue: not just talk. But deed and truth. Deed is the doing. Truth means the love is real, not a show, not a deed done to be seen. You can do a kind thing for a selfish reason; John wants both the hands and the heart. Notice the tender start: my little children. He's not scolding. He sounds like a grandfather. In the Catholic tradition, this is the ground of the works of mercy: feeding, clothing, visiting, sheltering. Love that has a shape you could photograph.

616.title: Perfect charity casts out fear (1 John 4:18)
616.howItsDone: Catholics count fear of the Lord, understood as reverent awe, among the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit received at confirmation, and the Church teaches that love for God frees a person from the servile fear of punishment.

segments.voice: Yesterday, splanchna: love in deed and in truth. Your line was in deed.

A four-year-old stands at the edge of a swimming pool, toes curled over the side, shivering. In the water, her father holds out his arms. Jump, he says. I've got you. She doesn't move. The water is deep and her stomach is a fist. Then she looks at his face instead of the water, and something shifts. She jumps. What changed wasn't the depth of the pool. It was where she was looking. Late in his first letter, John says something about fear that sounds almost too simple, until you watch a kid at the edge of a pool.
screen: `TOES CURLED OVER THE EDGE.` → `SHE LOOKS AT HIS FACE.` → `SHE JUMPS.`

segments.voice: The Douay-Rheims: "Fear is not in charity: but perfect charity casteth out fear, because fear hath pain. And he that feareth, is not perfected in charity." Charity is the old word for love here, from the Latin caritas, the self-giving love the Greek calls agape. Perfect means grown up, complete, come to its full size. And cast out is strong: the Greek says love throws fear outside, out the door. Why? Because, John says, fear hath pain. The Greek word points to punishment: the fear of someone waiting to be punished, who can't rest for wondering what's coming. That's no way to live with God, and John says love is the way out. Just before this, he says God is love, and right after, that we love because he first loved us. Fear goes when you look at his face instead of the water. Now, a careful point. The Catholic tradition doesn't say all fear of God disappears. It speaks of fear of the Lord as one of the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit: awe, reverence, not wanting to hurt someone you love. What love casts out is the other kind, the cringing fear of a slave. The Catechism borrows a picture from Saint Basil. You can stand before God like a slave, afraid of the whip. Like a hired hand, working for wages. Or like a child, who responds to the love of the one who first loved them. Only the third one jumps.

If you pray, look toward God, who first loved you; if not, picture the face that makes you brave.
